powerRankings.blurb: There's something special cooking within San Francisco's defense, a unit that has every excuse to be average, at best, but continues to exceed expectations. While the final score (32-29) doesn’t suggest it, Sunday’s win in Seattle was a defense-driven victory -- and a big one for the team's confidence as a true Super Bowl contender.

An early bye gave the Chiefs a chance to restructure after losing some receiving firepower in their most recent outing, but I admit I've wondered if they might have benefited more from a break later in the calendar. That's out of their control, of course, and as one of the most complete teams in the NFL, they hold their place on the podium.

A classic NFC West showdown between bitter foes saw the Seahawks come inches short of a first down in the final minute, crushing their comeback hopes against the 49ers and producing a fitting new chapter in the rivalry. Sam Darnold needs to clean up his play and Seattle's offense has some questions to answer (especially on the ground), but a narrow loss to the No. 1 team in my rankings doesn’t knock the 'Hawks down the board.

Sunday night's win felt larger than the average victory because of how Baltimore achieved it -- with a veteran backup at quarterback and no room for error -- underscoring the winning culture that has long carried this franchise to perennial success. The Ravens executed a game plan focused on limiting Bijan Robinson and found the juice to complete the comeback on the road, resulting in Jesse Minter's most impressive triumph to date.

Judging by his expression as the game ended -- after Cam Little's walk-off field goal -- Liam Coen knew his team was fortunate to beat the Eagles on Sunday in London. Jacksonville had to overcome some extenuating circumstances, including needing to use an emergency long-snapper (and thus, motivating Coen to go for it in goal-to-go situations). The wins all count the same, though, and the Jaguars were happy to add another to their tally, even if it required a bit of good luck at the end.

The Bills benefitted from some good special teams execution and the latest collection of Josh Allen feats of excellence on Monday night, riding their superstar quarterback’s running efforts and timely passing to an OT victory over the Rams that sure seemed destined to end in a loss. In the win, Buffalo started slowly, committed two turnovers that should have been significant (but weren’t due to Los Angeles’ own inability to capitalize), landed a few haymakers, received a few strong hooks, staggered but never fell, and ultimately prevailed by the final bell. The Bills have plenty to clean up (ball security for James Cook being one BIG issue), but this is a win that can inform a team of its potential and its mettle. Buffalo showed plenty of the latter in prime-time proving ground.

I know the Vikings have a truly special defense. I’d been wondering whether their offense would ever show up. We saw signs of it in the second half against the Saints, a stretch in which Kyler Murray dropped a pass over three defenders into Justin Jefferson's bucket for a touchdown and led an attack that scored 17 points in the final two quarters. There are still plenty of kinks to work out, but Murray is beginning to look more comfortable in Kevin O'Connell's system.

Denver notched a win on Sunday, but boy was it ugly. The Broncos finished with 224 total yards and required excellent field position in order to produce points (four of their five scoring drives started in Chargers territory). Sean Payton's takeover of play-calling produced some operational chaos along the sideline and a few strange game-management decisions in the second half. I expect that to improve over time, and eventually, perhaps this offense will creep closer toward the effectiveness of the defense, which deserves the credit for the comeback victory.

Games tend to get weird in Miami at this time of year, and there was a bit of that in Sunday's contest. But for the most part, the Bengals took care of business by relying on their most trusted leaders. Joe Burrow played well, Ja'Marr Chase made another ridiculous catch for a touchdown, Cincinnati's defensive front made life difficult for the Dolphins for a good chunk of the game, the rest of the unit capitalized on some Malik Willis mistakes, and the Bengals held on for a win that wasn't as close as the final score suggested. There is some underlying concern in the backfield, though, where backup Samaje Perine is beginning to look like the superior option to starter Chase Brown.

It took one wild win over the Bills to return the Patriots to excellence. They detonated the Raiders on Sunday, with fantastic offensive performances by Drake Maye, Efton Chism III, Kyle Williams, DeMario Douglas -- heck, just throw in every skill-position player. They all feasted in a game that saw New England finish with 536 yards of offense, pairing perfectly with a defense that put the clamps on Las Vegas early.

The Lions wiped the floor with the Cardinals over the final three quarters of Sunday's lopsided victory. Jared Goff distributed the ball among his many talented pass catchers, torching Arizona's undisciplined defense for 271 yards and three touchdowns. Most importantly, Detroit's defense finally showed up! We'll see if the latter holds with star safety Brian Branch nearing his return.

We learned that the Rams have rediscovered their offensive stride, for the most part (it took a while to get there Monday night). We also know they have problems stopping the run, and the back end of their defense cannot stop committing poorly timed penalties. Most of all, we learned that Sean McVay still hasn’t learned from his squad’s past special teams issues. His ultra-conservative approach to an endgame situation in overtime produced a comically predictable result (Harrison Mevis’ potential game-winner was blocked), and McVay’s team paid the price for his decision to take his foot off the accelerator when Tyler Bass nailed the game-winning kick for Buffalo. It didn’t have to end like that, but these Rams sure do deserve to be 2-3.

We learned on Sunday that Ben Johnson is not quarterback-proof. Tyson Bagent's rough day kneecapped Chicago's offense, which managed just 246 yards and couldn't keep up with Green Bay's suddenly explosive offense. Understandably, the Packers showed little respect for the Bears' secondary, which finally became the problem I thought it might be entering 2026, surrendering a 367-yard passing day that could be transformative for Jordan Love and Co. Caleb Williams can't return fast enough.

Carolina enjoyed the bye after a remarkable victory over the Lions on the Sunday night stage. Bryce Young's future contract is only getting more expensive with each outing, a good problem to have for a franchise that once worried it might have to go quarterback shopping again. A road date with the Eagles and a return home for a divisional showdown with Tampa Bay await.

Atlanta's transformation into an imposing offensive force with a sneaky-good defense fell apart in the second half Sunday night. The main cause: Michael Penix Jr.'s ribs injury, which eliminated his sharp passing from the equation late in the contest and led to backup Tua Tagovailoa taking over in overtime. It was also a night when Bijan Robinson wasn't quite the game-breaking back he'd been over the previous few weeks. Atlanta's inability to keep the Ravens out of the end zone late in the fourth quarter was disappointing, but Penix's injury is most concerning. Hopefully, this isn't something that lingers.

Now this is the Packers offense I expected to see in 2026. Perhaps it took the rivalry with Chicago to bring out the best in Green Bay, or maybe Jordan Love just needed to be asked to let it fly for an entire afternoon in order to extract the Pack from the mud. Either way, it worked wonderfully. Love delivered a fantastic performance, throwing for 367 yards and two majestic touchdowns to Christian Watson, demolishing a Bears team that couldn’t stop giving the ball to Green Bay’s suddenly feisty defense. Adding Micah Parsons into this equation soon makes the Packers one of the teams we must pay close attention to going forward.

Can a tie feel like a win? It sure did for New York, a team that overcame a two-touchdown deficit in the fourth to force overtime, appeared set to snatch victory from the jaws of defeat in the extra period, fumbled away that chance and somehow ended up leaving Landover without a win or loss. The Giants have plenty to clean up defensively after allowing Jayden Daniels to scramble for two touchdowns, but there was a lot of good in this game, too, including a strong second-half showing from Jameis Winston. That said, it’s still difficult to pin down this first-place club.

The Cowboys suffered a disastrous loss on Thursday night, falling to a previously winless Buccaneers team that had every reason to lay down in Arlington. Instead, Bucky Irving ran through Dallas’ defense, Jalon Daniels produced a creditable performance in place of Baker Mayfield, and the Cowboys’ typically-explosive offense mustered just 16 points. We know Dallas only has one path to victory -- light up the scoreboard -- and when that doesn’t work, it exposes the flaws in this club. It’s only one loss, but it eliminated much of my confidence in this team being a real contender.

The Raiders finally became the overmatched team we expected to see in 2026. Las Vegas’ defense couldn’t stop a nosebleed on Sunday, surrendering over 500 yards of offense to a unit that seemed lost just two weeks prior. An inability to protect Kirk Cousins (plus a continued lack of production from the ground game) prevented the offense from keeping up in a blowout loss. It’s certainly not time to consider benching Cousins for Fernando Mendoza, but the Raiders have officially encountered their first pothole and will need to divert accordingly in order to sustain the momentum built by a strong start.

It was an admittedly ugly game for both sides, but the Jets finally finished on the victorious side. The inclement weather may distort the overall evaluation of Sunday’s contest, but what’s undeniable was the effectiveness of New York’s aggressive pass rush, which piled up eight sacks and shut down Cleveland’s offense (save for one late touchdown drive). Braelon Allen and Garrett Wilson both thrived despite constant rain, two encouraging signs for a team that could use them going forward.

Cleveland’s method of leaning on defense and hoping the offense finds a fourth-quarter rhythm nearly worked out in the Browns’ favor, but a miserable sequence that included a regrettable-at-best approach while nursing a late lead, a botched snap on a punt and a disastrous final possession proved they can’t keep getting by with late-game heroics. They also still cannot run the ball, which won’t help matters in the future, no matter how effective rookie receiver Denzel Boston is in the second half.

Pittsburgh is becoming an every-other-week team, producing offensive explosions in odd-numbered weeks and struggling in even weeks. While that’s a path destined for a near-.500 record, perhaps Sunday’s output vs. Indianapolis was an example of a group recovering from a tough loss and applying the lessons learned. It was certainly encouraging to see the Steelers finally lean on Jaylen Warren. That’s a method that will produce consistent success, regardless of week number.

The Buccaneers began their climb out of the basement with an inspired performance in a game everyone expected them to lose, stifling Dallas’ offense while playing opportunistic defense. Bucky Irving finally found daylight, too, racking up 165 ground yards and propelling Tampa Bay’s offense with rookie undrafted free agent Jalon Daniels under center. Give the kid his flowers, too; Daniels turned in a strong performance that was better than his final stat line suggested. The Bucs just might be all right without Baker Mayfield.

The Colts are an underwhelming team right now because they put too much stock in a receiving corps led by Alec Pierce and Josh Downs, and only have Downs available to make a difference. Their offensive line has disappointed, too, and Lou Anarumo’s defensive reclamation project is still in its early stages. There are moments in which you see Indianapolis’ potential, and it battled in Sunday’s loss to Pittsburgh ... but predictably couldn’t finish drives. The result was not surprising, but each time I watch these Colts, it leaves me wondering what could be. At least Daniel Jones didn’t turn the ball over for a game.

Houston did what everyone expected it to do: take care of business against the worst team in the NFL. C.J. Stroud added another fruitful week to what is quickly becoming a very strong rebound season, the Texans finally got a little bit more out of their ground game (despite losing David Montgomery to injury), and the superior AFC South team walked away with an easy win. It’s a start, and we'll see what becomes of the Marvin Harrison Jr. trade, but it’s going to be a long climb out of 0-4.

Sunday's loss to Jacksonville had to hurt especially bad for the Eagles. Days after their legendary right tackle retired and front office traded away their starting center (who had moved to guard out of necessity), a banged-up Philly squad flew to London and nearly pulled off a remarkable win. The Eagles had overcome adversity, stood tall in the shadow of their own goal post and taken a late lead that left them poised to fly home as winners. The final kickoff, ensuing return and 57-yard Cam Little field goal wiped all of that out in a flash, sending the Eagles back to the same heartbreaking place in which they’ve resided for the last few weeks. Losses like this can send teams into tailspins. We’ll see if Nick Sirianni can prevent that from happening.

I’m losing faith in my pick to win the NFC South. I thought the Saints had enough defensively to keep Minnesota’s low-ceiling offense within reach, and also believed Tyler Shough was capable of getting the ball out consistently against the blitz. I was wrong. Shough finished with 96 passing yards, threw two interceptions and New Orleans' offense finished under 150 net yards against Brian Flores' fierce defense. This team doesn't seem quite ready for the big time.

Jayden Daniels returned and injected life into Washington’s offense, which was nice. The Commanders’ defense acquitted itself well, too, until the fourth-quarter collapse that saw Jameis Winston lead two touchdown drives to send the game to overtime. The ending wiped everything else away in the general football consciousness, which is understandable, but I liked what I saw from the Commanders for most of this game. That chaotic, disastrous finish was too fitting for this team, though, which is why it lands here after giving away a gift-wrapped win to take a painful tie.

First, the good: RB Ollie Gordon II has legitimate juice. The young playmakers out wide (plus TE Greg Dulcich) are fun to watch. LB Jacob Rodriguez is a stud who should be a front-runner for Defensive Rookie of the Year. Now, the bad: QB Malik Willis learned a hard lesson about not playing outside of his limits. Miami’s defensive weaknesses were still evident when Joe Burrow hit big plays and led steady scoring marches. The Dolphins are still winless. But for another week, they competed and didn’t make a ton of mistakes that would suggest a team headed into the abyss. That first win will come eventually.

If I could eject myself from the Chargers experience, I would. The banged-up offensive line can’t protect Justin Herbert, who can’t keep himself from continuing to make mistakes. He’s loose with the ball under pressure (leading to the costly fumble we saw in the fourth quarter), his processing seems to be damaged by the weekly struggles (seen in the late interception he threw directly to Brandon Jones), and there’s no clear path out of this mess. The Bolts gave away a winnable game Sunday, one in which they appeared poised to prevail before self-destructing in spectacular fashion. This isn’t your typical Chargering; it’s much, much worse.

In the first few weeks of this season, the Cardinals ostensibly proved they could score enough to keep up with most teams, even if their defense couldn’t do its part. That seemed to position them well against a Lions team that dragged a porous defense through the opening month, but that just wasn't the case on Sunday in the desert. Arizona scored once, then went completely quiet, reducing its offense to a chuck-and-pray approach on third-and-long and completely eliminating Jeremiyah Love from the game plan because of the score difference. With all due respect to Jacoby Brissett, you’re not going to win many games when he’s averaging 40 throws per outing.

At this point, Titans fans probably would like to simulate to the offseason. The offense carries the lowest potential in the NFL (it's 32nd in yards per game by nearly 16 yards), the defense has far too much responsibility to carry on a weekly basis, and folks are starting to ask if Cam Ward is going to get benched. These are the themes that surface when a team is trudging toward a top-five pick in April, an experience that is becoming all too familiar in Nashville.
